KEY MESSAGE 1...Warm and humid conditions combined with a front will lead
to severe storms across parts of area through this evening.

Turning active this afternoon and evening as spokes of shortwave 
energy/outflows ahead of an incoming cold front pass through the 
region. A Severe Thunderstorm Watch will likely be issued for 
portions of Maryland, northern-central VA, and the eastern WV 
Panhandle. Storms look to initialize along the bay breeze 
toward Baltimore/northeast MD and along a spoke of shortwave 
energy pivoting between I-81 and the Blue Ridge between now-4pm 
as the capping inversion buckles. Expect scattered to broken 
lines or clusters of convection pushing northeast from the Blue 
Ridge/I-81 impacting a large chunk of the metros between 5-9pm. 
Not everyone will see the storms this afternoon and evening, but
something to monitor; especially if you have plans outdoors. 

Hi-res guidance continues to struggle a bit in the evolution of 
storms this afternoon given the capping inversion and a outflow 
boundary zipping southwest from southern NJ/DE down along the 
western shore of the Chesapeake Bay. The lead shortwave is up across 
southern/central NJ with a secondary shortwave in the vicinity of 
southwest and central VA, and the main cold front back toward the 
Ohio River. It's a matter of how these remaining pieces of energy 
and lifting mechanisms interact, especially through the remaining 
peak heating period for severe weather development. 

Damaging winds will be the main threat with storms today given 30-35 
kts of deep layer shear and modest instability values up of 1000 
j/kg. Moderate mid level lapse rates (7-8 C/km), strong winds in the 
upper atmosphere, and relatively light low level winds could also 
result in some severe level hail. As mentioned in previous 
forecasts, hi-res model guidance is still depicting some decent low-
level curvature to hodographs, especially along the MD/PA border in 
northeast MD (due to perhaps a bay breeze/outflow from decaying
storms over southern NJ) which may increase low level shear. 
The Storm Prediction Center continues a Slight Risk (Level 2 out
of 5) for severe weather through this evening. 

Heavy rainfall will remain a concern given multiple rounds of 
convection, especially over central and northeast MD where residual 
outflow boundaries could slow up convection. Given relatively 
unidirectional flow relative to the surface trough could result 
in some training (hinted at by splotches of higher QPF in some 
CAMs from Baltimore/Annapolis, MD points northeast; a secondary 
area down around Fredericksburg/Stafford/Culpeper, VA). No Flood
Watches are planned at this time, but will need to be monitor 
given PWATS over 1.5"+ and likely rain rates of 0.50-1" in a 
30-45 minute period. While some showers and storms may linger 
into the night, the severe weather threat should be winding down
after 9-10pm.

The slow moving cold front will bisect the area Friday morning while 
the mid/upper level trough lags to the west. As a result, expect 
additional showers and thunderstorms during the peak heating period, 
especially along and south of the front. Highest probabilities for 
severe weather appear to be south of I-66/US-50 across southern MD, 
the VA Piedmont, and northern neck of VA. Damaging winds will be the 
main threat along with locally heavy rainfall. Coverage once again 
will be scattered, but highly dependent on where the front resides 
and if any cloud cover lingers across the region. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry conditions this weekend with increasingly hot 
and humid conditions through next week.

A cold front pushes through the area early Saturday morning, likely 
stalling just south across southern VA to the Carolinas this 
weekend. Surface high pressure builds south into the Mid-Atlantic as 
winds shift quickly from north to easterly on Saturday. The high 
moves offshore Sunday, bringing the return of southerly winds. While 
we remain under broad troughing aloft, the presence of drier air at 
the surface will keep rain chances out of the forecast. Lingering 
humidity and building heat make for a warm and muggy weekend as 
highs reach the 80s to around 90F.

Models are generally in good agreement that a strong mid-level ridge 
builds across the southern U.S. and into the Mid-Atlantic during the 
early to middle part of next week. This brings us well above normal 
temperatures for late August as highs reach the low to mid 90s. Hot 
and humid conditions are likely as heat indices reach to the low 
100s east of the Blue Ridge. 

A series of mid-level disturbances will ride along the top of the 
ridge from the northern High Plains to the Northeast next week. 
Depending on the exact position of the ridge, some of these 
disturbances could be near or over our area come the middle to late 
part of the week. For now, Monday and Tuesday look mostly dry, 
though cannot rule out a stray thunderstorm or two given the 
humid/unstable atmosphere. By Wed
